KEPLER_5 – Exploring Beyond Boundaries

KEPLER_5 is a team of passionate innovators driven by curiosity and a vision for space exploration. Through the Space Mission Design Game, we aim to design creative space missions, develop strategic solutions, and explore the possibilities of interplanetary travel. .KEPLER_5 – Dream Beyond Earth. Design Beyond Limits.
summary:
ORBITX is an interactive space mission design and simulation platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It lets anyone experience what it takes to plan, build, and run a real space mission, all from the browser.

Pick a destination, whether the Moon, Mars, Venus, an asteroid, or Jupiter, then set your scientific objectives. From there, you design your own spacecraft by choosing propulsion systems, power sources, communication equipment, thermal protection, and science instruments. Every choice has consequences. You'll need to balance mass, fuel, power, communications, spacecraft health, and budget while guiding your mission through each stage and handling unexpected anomalies along the way.

To keep things grounded in reality, ORBITX integrates NASA/JPL Horizons data, giving you real planetary positions and velocities rather than made-up numbers.

We built ORBITX because space engineering often feels out of reach. By turning complex mission design into a hands on experience, it helps students understand real world engineering trade offs, sharpen their problem solving skills, and test different strategies. Best of all, they can learn from both successes and failures in a risk free virtual environment, just like real mission teams do.
details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work?

ORBITX is a web based space mission design and simulation platform that lets you experience an entire mission, from the first sketch to the final report.

You start by choosing a destination: the Moon, Mars, Venus, an asteroid, or Jupiter. Then you set your scientific objectives and build your spacecraft piece by piece, picking the structural frame, propulsion system, power source, communication antenna, thermal protection, battery, and science instruments.

Behind the scenes, ORBITX runs engineering calculations covering mass, propellant needs, delta-v, power generation, communication capacity, thermal conditions, radiation protection, and budget. If your design passes these checks, you launch it.

From there, you guide the mission through each stage, watch simulated telemetry, and deal with unexpected anomalies as they appear. At the end, you get a mission report and a performance score.

To keep things grounded in reality, ORBITX pulls planetary positions and velocities from NASA/JPL Horizons, linking the simulation to actual astronomical data.

2. What benefits does the project provide?

  • Interactive learning: Complex aerospace concepts become easier to grasp through hands-on experimentation.
  • Engineering awareness: Users see how changing one component ripples through the entire spacecraft.
  • Safe experimentation: Try different designs and learn from failed missions without any real-world risk.
  • Scientific understanding: Introduces planetary exploration, science instruments, orbital information, and mission objectives.
  • Decision-making skills: Users make engineering choices while working within limited resources and budgets.
  • Accessibility: It runs in the browser, so anyone can explore mission design without expensive labs or hardware.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our main goal is to make space mission engineering more accessible, engaging, and easy to understand, especially for students and space enthusiasts.

ORBITX bridges the gap between textbook aerospace theory and practical mission planning. When users see how spacecraft design, scientific objectives, resource management, and mission outcomes connect, they naturally think more critically, creatively, and analytically.

We hope the experience sparks curiosity and inspires more students to pursue aerospace engineering, space science, physics, and other STEM fields.

4. What technologies and tools did we use?

We built ORBITX with a modern web stack.

Frontend and interface

  • React.js for the interactive UI
  • TypeScript for type safe application logic
  • Tailwind CSS for styling and responsive layouts
  • Three.js and React Three Fiber for 3D space visualizations
  • Recharts for telemetry and performance charts
  • Framer Motion for interface animations

Backend and data

  • Node.js and Express.js for the server and API
  • MongoDB and Mongoose for storing mission data
  • NASA/JPL Horizons API for planetary ephemeris data

Development and testing

  • Visual Studio Code as our editor
  • Vite for development and builds
  • Vitest for testing simulation and engineering logic
  • Git and GitHub for version control and collaboration

ORBITX is fully software-based and needs no specialized hardware.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

ORBITX brings together space exploration, spacecraft engineering, interactive simulation, and game-based learning in one platform.

Instead of just reading about planets and spacecraft, users become mission designers, and every decision has consequences. A more powerful instrument adds mass and power demand. Electric propulsion saves propellant but needs far more electrical power. Distant planets bring tougher challenges with communication, radiation, and available solar energy.

We also added mission anomalies, multiple difficulty levels, performance scoring, achievements, and interactive 3D solar-system visualizations to keep things engaging.

Finally, integrating NASA/JPL Horizons data ties real planetary information into the learning experience, so the simulation feels authentic rather than purely fictional.

6. What factors did our team consider?

While building ORBITX, we thought carefully about what makes a mission both realistic and fun to learn from:

  • Scientific objectives: Instruments must support the chosen mission goals.
  • Mass and payload: The spacecraft must stay within the launch vehicle's capacity.
  • Propulsion and fuel: Propellant is estimated with the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation.
  • Power management: Electrical demand must be balanced against generation.
  • Communication: The antenna must be able to support the mission.
  • Thermal and radiation protection: Temperature swings and radiation levels vary by destination.
  • Budget: Component, launcher, and operating costs all count.
  • Mission reliability: Unexpected events and spacecraft health keep every flight unpredictable.
  • Data accuracy and transparency: We use NASA/JPL Horizons for ephemeris data and openly document the assumptions and limits of our educational models.
  • User experience: The interface is intuitive and visually engaging, even for beginners.

Conclusion

ORBITX turns the complexity of space mission planning into a hands-on experience. By combining real planetary data, simplified engineering models, spacecraft configuration, and mission simulation, it lets users design, experiment, make tough calls, and learn how real missions depend on carefully balanced systems.
